summary: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, submitted to the International Journal of Forecasting

title: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
summary: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a factor of 2.5 and removes that remaining violation. The gain costs a small and deliberate concession in raw deterrence. Twin inference meets the 50 ms budget on a workstation core and an embedded GPU, and is projected to meet it on both edge CPUs when the three envelope stages are evaluated in a single batched call; the complete decision-to-enforcement path was measured only on the workstation.

title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
summary: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.

title: Block diagonal preconditioners for arrow-shaped multiple saddle-point linear systems
summary: We consider multiple saddle-point linear systems with block-arrow structure. We analyze exact and inexact Schur complement based block diagonal preconditioner, by characterizing the eigenvalues of the preconditioned matrices in terms of the zeros of specific rational functions. Numerical results onto large tests coming from liquid crystal modeling and PDE-constrained optimization validate the obtained eigenvalue bounds

title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

title: Simultaneous energy and entropy stability of volume-penalisation immersed-boundary methods for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations
summary: Immersed-boundary methods avoid body-fitted meshes, but the energy or entropy stability of the underlying flow discretisation does not automatically extend to the immersed treatment. This manuscript analyses the volume-penalised compressible Navier--Stokes equations for both energy and entropy stability, on the continuous and semi-discrete levels, and integrates the isolated source exactly in time. The source is formulated as a one-parameter family indexed by $θ$, whose momentum component relaxes the fluid velocity towards the prescribed solid velocity; $θ$ sets how much of the resulting kinetic-energy loss leaves the domain rather than being converted to internal energy. The two stability requirements impose opposing bounds on $θ$, with dissipation of the relative total energy requiring $θ\geq0$ and stability of the mathematical entropy requiring $θ\leq1$. Where penalisation acts, both conditions are therefore satisfied if and only if $0\leqθ\leq1$, and the symmetric value $θ=1/2$ divides the kinetic-energy loss equally between the domain and the internal energy. We conclude that any entropy-stable split-form discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method remains semi-discretely entropy stable once the source is added at the collocation nodes, for stationary and prescribed moving bodies alike.

title: Numerical simulation of biological capsules based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes
summary: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for the simulation of biological capsules based on meshes that adapt iteration-wise to the shape of the membrane. The discretization leverages a Hybrid High Order method (HHO) to solve a Stokes problem with a source term distributed on the interface between the internal and the external phases. The HHO discretization supports meshes composed of general polygons, permitting to use fitted meshes that can be easily generated by cutting the elements intersected by the interface. Moreover, polygonal meshes allow arbitrarily accurate interface discretizations without introducing bulk degrees of freedom. The presentation of the simulation algorithm is completed with a proof-of-concept numerical test on a well-established benchmark: the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow.

title: Hyperelastic Modeling of Cardiac Tissue Deformation for Data Registration
summary: This work proposes a biomechanical registration framework designed to combine functional optical-mapping data with structural high-resolution MRI of cardiac tissue. The two acquisitions are performed in different mechanical configurations: optical mapping is obtained after stretching the sample, whereas MRI is acquired in a fixed resting state. To estimate the deformation between these configurations, the tissue is modeled as a nearly incompressible transversely isotropic hyperelastic material, and the traction amplitude is identified from optical-map marker positions through an inverse problem. Two-and threedimensional simulations show physically admissible deformations and provide a first proof of concept for the proposed strategy.

title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations
summary: In this work, we develop low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations and incorporate them into a basis-update \& Galerkin mass-lumped finite element method (\mbox{BUG-MLFEM}). By incorporating mass lumping via Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, the spatial discretization yields a matrix differential equation equipped with diagonal positive-definite mass matrices. We establish the weighted dynamical low-rank approximation (WDLRA) within the Galerkin framework of the MLFEM system, proving the theoretical equivalence between the BUG integrator and MLFEM on low-rank subspaces, which guarantees the discrete well-posedness of the implicit BUG steps. To overcome the severe computational bottleneck of standard $O(m^3+n^3)$ Sylvester solvers, we develop tailored, low-cost non-iterative solvers that exploit the inherent sparse-by-small algebraic structure. Under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions (BCs), the large coefficient matrices are banded, enabling efficient diagonalization of the small $r \times r$ factor matrix and reducing the per-step computational complexity to $O((m+n)r^2)$ and storage to $O((m+n)r)$. For periodic BCs, we combine this diagonalization strategy with a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update to handle wrap-around corner entries at negligible additional cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate first-order temporal and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence of the proposed BUG-MLFEM in the discrete $L^2$ norm, where $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the finite element space, together with significant computational speedups over existing low-rank integrators.

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
summary: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

title: A two-level preconditioner for discontinuous virtual element methods with irregular subdomains
summary: We introduce and analyze a two-level overlapping additive Schwarz preconditioner for discontinuous Galerkin discretizations of virtual element spaces on general polygonal meshes in two dimensions, for a second-order elliptic problem whose coefficient is constant on each subdomain and may have large jumps across the interface. The discretization is a weighted symmetric interior penalty formulation: the averages carry the coefficient and the penalty is scaled by its harmonic mean across each edge, which keeps the method consistent and makes the constants of the analysis independent of the coefficient. The coarse space is obtained from a virtual, continuous partition of unity with a single degree of freedom per subdomain vertex, and is therefore applicable to the irregular subdomains produced by a graph partitioner; the discrete harmonic extension used to build it may be replaced by a cheaper projection onto polynomials of low degree. We prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $C(1+\log(H/h))(1+H/δ)$, where $H$, $h$ and $δ$ denote the subdomain diameter, the mesh size and the overlap, and where $C$ is independent of the number of subdomains and of the contrast of the coefficient, provided the latter is quasi-monotone. This is the same bound known for the conforming case and the analysis allows for hanging nodes. We also show, by an explicit example, that the quasi-monotonicity assumption cannot be dispensed with. Numerical experiments with structured triangular, hexagonal and Voronoi meshes, and with subdomains obtained both by uniform partitioning and by METIS, confirm the theory.

title: Fully discrete multi-entropy-stable compact Runge--Kutta discontinuous Galerkin methods for hyperbolic conservation laws
summary: We develop fully discrete multi-entropy-stable high-order compact Runge--Kutta discontinuous Galerkin (cRKDG) methods for hyperbolic conservation laws. Our main result is a weak cell entropy inequality for multi-dimensional systems after one full high-order Runge--Kutta (RK) time step. The proof exploits the cell-local intermediate stages of cRKDG: their perturbations are controlled by the initial in-cell variation. The analysis does not require a strong stability preserving decomposition or stagewise entropy correction. For a sufficiently dissipative Lax--Friedrichs flux and explicit RK methods with nonnegative output weights, the inequality holds under a suitable time-step restriction for strongly convex entropy pairs. For a prescribed, uniformly conditioned family of such entropies, common dissipation and time-step conditions ensure weak cell entropy stability for all entropy pairs. A single cell-average-preserving scaling at the end of each step then enforces all corresponding strong cell entropy inequalities simultaneously. We also prove a Lax--Wendroff-type theorem: under the stated assumptions, any strongly convergent sequence of numerical solutions converges to a weak solution satisfying all prescribed entropy inequalities. Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions demonstrate high-order accuracy, the benefit of multiple entropy constraints for nonconvex scalar problems, and robust performance on shock problems.

title: Global Regularization of the Spatial Elliptic Restricted Three-body Problem: Quaternionic, Hamiltonian Formulation
summary: Any objects in space may encounter singularity due to the inverse-square law of the gravitational force, hindering the analysis and propagation of particle motion in space. Regularization in celestial mechanics removes such gravitational singularities in equations of motion by transforming the time and coordinates. This paper addresses a class of regularization methods known as global regularization for restricted three-body problems (R3BPs), which simultaneously removes the two singularities (e.g., Earth and Moon in cislunar space). It enables analysis, propagation, and prediction of particle motion throughout the domain of R3BPs, which is in stark contrast to regularizing each singularity individually. In particular, this paper develops a formulation for global regularization of the spatial elliptic R3BP (ER3BP) under external perturbations. The presented formulation leverages mathematical tools from quaternionic (hyper-complex) algebra and Hamiltonian mechanics. This approach enables us to (i) elegantly handle the four-dimensional coordinates arising from the dimension-lifting operation for spatial regularization, (ii) systematically derive the coordinate-momentum transformation while preserving the canonical structure and incorporating perturbing forces, and (iii) provide geometric insights for analyzing the regularity of the transformation, resulting Hamiltonian, and dynamical flow. Numerical examples demonstrate the validity of the mathematical results as well as significant numerical benefits of the regularization formulation in perturbed Earth-Moon ER3BP.

title: A Unified Framework for Randomized Row-Action Methods for Structured Data Fitting and Constraint Geometry
summary: We study randomized row-action methods for problems with linear observations, convex constraints, and non-Euclidean geometry. Our starting point is a unified formulation in which the data-fitting term acts in observation space, while the feasible set and the regularizer encode structure in variable space. It covers constrained least squares, nonnegative and simplex-constrained models, regularized data fitting, and equality-constrained Bregman selection problems. The structure of these problems leads naturally to two algorithmic branches. The first uses primal Bregman-proximal row steps for soft data-fitting problems. The second uses dual Bregman--Kaczmarz steps for problems with hard equality constraints. We first derive a common one-step inequality. We then give deterministic and stochastic convergence results for the soft branch under relative smoothness. For constrained least squares, the normalized row oracle has exact first- and second-moment identities. They yield an expected ergodic bound in the inconsistent case, an $O(1/K)$ bound in the interpolating case, and linear convergence of the actual iterates under a residual error bound. For equality-constrained selectors, we prove linear convergence in expected Bregman distance under a residual-to-Bregman error bound. We recall global sufficient conditions for this bound and derive local constants for the nonnegative quadratic geometry and the entropy geometry on the simplex. Numerical experiments illustrate the noisy stepsize trade-off and the local entropy selector theory, and show that entropic row-action updates can recover interpretable factors in a simplex-structured nonnegative matrix factorization problem.

title: A quantum algorithm for meshless lattice Boltzmann method with unitary interpolation
summary: We present a mass-weighted meshless formulation for the shifted incompressible lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) whose streaming step is exactly unitary, combining with the Carleman embedding. In traditional meshless LBM, on a scattered node set the semi-Lagrangian streaming step is an interpolation, which is not unitary; a generic block encoding of this matrix therefore requires a normalization proportional to its sparsity and logarithmically many ancillas. To overcome the non-unitarity, we instead express the interpolation as the exponential exp(a Dx + b Dy) of mimetic derivative operators. Endowing each node with its Voronoi mass and applying a mass-weighted similarity transform renders these derivative operators skew-Hermitian by enforcing moment constraints together with low-wave number trigonometric differentiation conditions, so that the interpolation becomes exactly unitary. Such unitarization of interpolation leave the local collision step unchanged up to a rescaling of its quadratic term, where the same weights define the amplitude encoding of the distribution functions. For quasi-uniform node sets, the mass-weighting diagonal remains within a unit-order normalization that degrades only mildly as the Carleman truncation order grows, thereby mitigating the cost of block encoding. Numerical experiments on the Taylor Green vortex confirm that the method reproduces the full meshless LBM, with the velocity error decreasing as the Carleman order increases.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo for Zeroth-Order Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Inexact Lower Level Solves
summary: Variational regularization techniques are dominant in the field of mathematical imaging. The expressiveness of these methods heavily depends on the adopted regularization formulation which usually involves a number of parameters which have to be fine-tuned by the user. To circumvent the heavy computational costs associated with this parameter tuning, data-driven learning strategies have turned out to be a useful strategy. Selecting parameters by learning from data gives rise to a hierarchical (bilevel) optimization problem, which is in general computationally hard to solve. Our aim in this paper is to develop a data-efficient solution strategy for the bilevel learning problem. To that end, we propose a multilevel Monte Carlo derivative-free optimization method that couples Gaussian smoothing of the upper-level objective (parameter selection) with a hierarchy of lower-level (variational regularization) solution accuracies. Being agnostic towards the specific way the lower-level problem is solved, we derive explicit oracle complexity and computational cost statements for approximately solving the entire bilevel learning problem. Our statements are parameterized by the employed lower-level solution method, thus allowing for a direct cost accounting from the variational reconstruction method to the parameter selection problem. This enables us to give a universal end-to-end complexity analysis of bilevel learning, valid for the most important optimization routines in inverse problems, rather than for a specific choice of methods.

title: KKT Residual Sliding Manifolds: A Projection-Free Structured Finite-Time Solver for Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation
summary: Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation (NCO) requires simultaneous satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Existing methods enforce these conditions through projections, penalties, barriers, or sequential approximations, potentially introducing computational complexity and convergence difficulties. For nonconvex problems, a KKT point need not be a local optimum. This paper reformulates NCO as stabilisation of a unified KKT sliding residual manifold and develops SM-KKT, a projection-free solver. Stationarity, equality feasibility, and regularised Fischer-Burmeister complementarity are integrated into a unified residual system, with complementarity encoding inequality feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness. The manifold's zero set is shown to be equivalent to the KKT conditions. The required Jacobian saddle-point inertia is characterised and shown, under stated assumptions, to be equivalent to the simultaneous satisfaction of the Linear Independence Constraint Qualification (LICQ) and Second-Order Sufficient Condition (SOSC). This characterisation establishes local stability of the structured correction algorithm under these conditions and distinguishes nondegenerate locally optimal KKT solutions from points failing second-order optimality. SM-KKT computes structured primal--dual corrections and applies a discrete sliding reaching law to drive the KKT residual into a prescribed boundary layer in finite time. Four nonlinear benchmarks show recovery of reference constrained optima with KKT residuals below $10^{-6}$, earlier boundary-layer reaching, and favourable KKT accuracy compared with projected primal-dual, augmented-Lagrangian, quadratic-penalty, and log-barrier baselines.

title: (Super-)fast convergence rates for Chernoff approximations via centered differences and Richardson extrapolation
summary: We use centered differences to construct Chernoff families and derive even asymptotic expansions for their iterated products. Richardson extrapolation is then used to cancel polynomial part and thereby raise the convergence order. As illustrations, we apply the construction to uniformly parabolic, Schrödinger-type second-order operators and to a third-order dispersive operator, obtaining, at extrapolation depth $m$, the rates $ O(n^{-2m}) $ on the Sobolev scales $H^{2m+δ}$, $H^{4m}$, and $H^{5m}$, respectively, with arbitrary $δ>0$. In the analytic category, quantitative all-order estimates allow the extrapolation depth to grow with the base resolution and yield the super-fast rates $e^{-cn^2}$ for the two second-order models and $e^{-cn} $ for the third-order model. The constructions are explicit in terms of the coefficients of the underlying differential operators and do not use the target semigroup in their definition. This provides a constructive positive answer to the challenge of super-fast Chernoff approximation formulated by Remizov in Problem 30 of arXiv:2410.00416.

title: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method for the shallow water equations on Cartesian grids: mass conservation and wetting and drying over variable topography
summary: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method is proposed for the two-dimensional shallow water equations with a variable bed (topography), solved with an explicit Godunov-type finite volume scheme (unsplit second-order MUSCL, HLLC flux, hydrostatic reconstruction) on Cartesian grids. Ghost-cell methods leak mass through the wall. To find a robust and conservative treatment, eight constructions of the ghost values and a cut-cell form of the continuity equation were applied to seven test problems, which include wetting and drying on sloping beds and a laboratory dam break. In the resulting scheme, the ghost values are interpolated bilinearly at the image point; solid and dry nodes are excluded, and the weights of the remaining nodes are renormalized. Mass is conserved by solving the continuity equation in cut-cell form, while the momentum equations are left unchanged. The proposed scheme is about as accurate as the ghost-cell method without this modification and preserves a lake at rest whose shoreline crosses an immersed wall. Because only the continuity equation is modified, it avoids the treatment of the momentum equations on cut cells (wall pressure, cell merging) that a full cut-cell method requires.

title: Preconditioned Latent Variable Proximal Point Method for Optimal Control Problems with Control Constraints
summary: The latent variable proximal point (LVPP) method solves optimization problems in function spaces with pointwise constraints by a sequence of smooth subproblems whose iterates are strictly feasible. We apply it to linear-quadratic elliptic optimal control problems. Control and observation are distributed but may be restricted to subdomains. We prove that the LVPP subproblems are well posed in appropriate function spaces, that the iteration converges for every sequence of proximity parameters with divergent sum, and that it delivers the Lagrange multiplier of the constraint as a by-product. We interpret the Newton step for the LVPP subproblem as a linear-quadratic optimal control problem with a spatially varying control cost, and we show that Newton's method converges locally quadratically. The Newton systems are solved by the minimal residual method with a block-diagonal preconditioner. We prove that the spectrum of the Newton operator with respect to the inner product defined by the preconditioner is bounded independently of the proximity parameter, the iterate, the mesh and the observation and control domains. The results are combined into a complete algorithm, and tested in numerical experiments.

title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
comments: Accepted at ICONIP 2026 (33rd International Conference on Neural Information Processing)
summary: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
comment: Accepted at ICONIP 2026 (33rd International Conference on Neural Information Processing)

title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
comments: 32 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables, 116 references; supplementary information (15 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables) included in the same PDF. Code and data available on request
summary: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.
comment: 32 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables, 116 references; supplementary information (15 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables) included in the same PDF. Code and data available on request

title: Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
summary: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
summary: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) enforce such requirements with a semidefinite program that minimally modifies a nominal control input. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
summary: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

title: Compositional Sensitivity Analysis for Multiobjective System Co-Design
summary: Sensitivity analysis of coupled systems typically propagates derivatives of single-valued maps, whereas multiobjective optimization generally treats sensitivity at the system level rather than through interconnected subsystems. We develop a mathematical framework for compositional sensitivity analysis in multiobjective system design, building on monotone co-design. Subsystems are represented as design problems (DPs), interconnected through series, parallel, union, intersection, and feedback composition. We introduce tangential DPs (TDPs) to describe first-order variations around an operating point, show that they preserve the structure of DPs, and characterize their queries through graphical derivatives. To account for multiple internal realizations of a system-level operating point, tangential co-design problems compose families of local TDPs by taking a union over these realizations while retaining the original interconnection structure. We show that these compositions yield families of TDPs and establish conditions under which sensitivity analysis commutes with individual composition operations. Beyond infinitesimal sensitivity, we show that bounded tangential models of convex DPs provide tighter outer approximations of feasible finite changes, which can be propagated through co-design problems without union compositions. We conclude with several convex and nonconvex numerical examples that showcase the framework's accuracy and computational benefits.

title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
comments: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026), Hawaii, USA
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026), Hawaii, USA

title: Multiclass histogram-based thresholding using kernel density estimation and scale-space representations
summary: We present a method for multiclass thresholding of histograms whose modes may overlap so strongly that they merge into a unimodal distribution. The histogram is approximated by a nonparametric kernel density (KD) estimate, a mixture of Gaussians with one component per bin and a common bandwidth, whose parameters are determined by Expectation-Maximization (EM) iterations. Because the estimate is a Gaussian mixture, the semigroup property of Gaussian convolution yields its scale-space representation in closed form, at bandwidths both larger and smaller than the fitted one. The algorithm increases or decreases the bandwidth until the number of local minima of the estimate equals the number of requested classes minus one, and returns the positions of those minima as the threshold values. We validate the method on synthetic histograms with known thresholds, and we apply it to the histogram of X-ray computed tomography images of a natural porous sample in which the three phases strongly overlap. The porosity computed from the resulting segmentation agrees with the direct experimental measurement to within 4%, whereas K-means clustering misestimates it by 52%.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cardiac Segmentation: Towards Structure Mutual Information Maximization
comments: CVPR Workshop Paper. v4: Revised the theoretical analysis and its proof (Theorem 1, supplementary material); unified notation; fixed description errors
summary: Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches have recently succeeded in various medical image segmentation tasks. The reported works often tackle the domain shift problem by aligning the domain-invariant features and minimizing the domain-specific discrepancies. That strategy works well when the difference between a specific domain and between different domains is slight. However, the generalization ability of these models on diverse imaging modalities remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces UDA-VAE++, an unsupervised domain adaptation framework for cardiac segmentation. We show that the evidence lower bound of VAE-based domain adaptation penalizes the mutual information between the image and the latent space, including the structure information that segmentation relies on. Maximizing the structure mutual information removes this penalty on the structure information, while the remaining information is still compressed. To estimate this term, we develop a novel Structure Mutual Information Estimation (SMIE) block with a global estimator, a local estimator, and a prior information matching estimator to maximize the mutual information between the reconstruction and segmentation tasks. Specifically, we design a novel sequential reparameterization scheme that enables information flow and variance correction from the low-resolution latent space to the high-resolution latent space. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark cardiac segmentation datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art qualitatively and quantitatively. The code is available at https://github.com/LOUEY233/Toward-Mutual-Information
comment: CVPR Workshop Paper. v4: Revised the theoretical analysis and its proof (Theorem 1, supplementary material); unified notation; fixed description errors

title: Application based Evaluation of an Efficient Spike-Encoder, "Spiketrum"
comments: Under review in "IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence"
summary: Spike-based encoders represent information as sequences of spikes or pulses, which are transmitted between neurons. A prevailing consensus suggests that spike-based approaches demonstrate exceptional capabilities in capturing the temporal dynamics of neural activity and have the potential to provide energy-efficient solutions for low-power applications. The Spiketrum encoder efficiently compresses input data using spike trains or code sets (for non-spiking applications) and is adaptable to both hardware and software implementations, with lossless signal reconstruction capability. The paper proposes and assesses Spiketrum's hardware, evaluating its output under varying spike rates and its classification performance with popular spiking and non-spiking classifiers, and also assessing the quality of information compression and hardware resource utilization. The paper extensively benchmarks both Spiketrum hardware and its software counterpart against state-of-the-art, biologically-plausible encoders. The evaluations encompass benchmarking criteria, including classification accuracy, training speed, and sparsity when using encoder outputs in pattern recognition and classification with both spiking and non-spiking classifiers. Additionally, they consider encoded output entropy and hardware resource utilization and power consumption of the hardware version of the encoders. Results demonstrate Spiketrum's superiority in most benchmarking criteria, making it a promising choice for various applications. It efficiently utilizes hardware resources with low power consumption, achieving high classification accuracy. This work also emphasizes the potential of encoders in spike-based processing to improve the efficiency and performance of neural computing systems.
comment: Under review in "IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence"

title: Age of Trust (AoT): A Continuous Verification Framework for Wireless Networks
comments: This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE TMC
summary: Zero Trust is a new security vision for 6G networks that emphasises the philosophy of never trust and always verify. However, there is a fundamental trade-off between the wireless transmission efficiency and the trust level, which is reflected by the verification interval and its adaptation strategy. More importantly, the mathematical framework to characterise the trust level of the adaptive verification strategy is still missing. Inspired by this vision, we propose a concept called age of trust (AoT) to capture the characteristics of the trust level degrading over time, with the definition of the time elapsed since the last verification of the target user's trust plus the initial age, which depends on the trust level evaluated at that verification. The higher the trust level, the lower the initial age. To evaluate the trust level in the long term, the average AoT is used. We then investigate how to find a compromise between average AoT and wireless transmission efficiency with limited resources. In particular, we address the bi-objective optimization (BOO) problem between average AoT and throughput over a single link with arbitrary service process, where the identity of the receiver is constantly verified, and we devise a periodic verification scheme and a Q-learning-based scheme for constant process and random process, respectively. We also tackle the BOO problem in a multiple random access scenario, where a trust-enhanced frame-slotted ALOHA is designed. Finally, the numerical results show that our proposals can achieve a fair compromise between trust level and wireless transmission efficiency, and thus have a wide application prospect in various zero-trust architectures.
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE TMC

title: Scale-specific auxiliary multi-task contrastive learning for deep liver vessel segmentation
comments: 5 pages, 5 figures, IEEE ISBI 2023. v2: fixed a figure reference. Code for the multi-scale vessel clustering (Sect. 2.1): https://github.com/asadikine/vessel-scale-clustering
summary: Extracting hepatic vessels from abdominal images is of high interest for clinicians since it allows to divide the liver into functionally-independent Couinaud segments. In this respect, an automated liver blood vessel extraction is widely summoned. Despite the significant growth in performance of semantic segmentation methodologies, preserving the complex multi-scale geometry of main vessels and ramifications remains a major challenge. This paper provides a new deep supervised approach for vessel segmentation, with a strong focus on representations arising from the different scales inherent to the vascular tree geometry. In particular, we propose a new clustering technique to decompose the tree into various scale levels, from tiny to large vessels. Then, we extend standard 3D UNet to multi-task learning by incorporating scale-specific auxiliary tasks and contrastive learning to encourage the discrimination between scales in the shared representation. Promising results, depicted in several evaluation metrics, are revealed on the public 3D-IRCADb dataset.
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, IEEE ISBI 2023. v2: fixed a figure reference. Code for the multi-scale vessel clustering (Sect. 2.1): https://github.com/asadikine/vessel-scale-clustering

title: Towards Dependable Optical Flow: Benchmarks for Real-World Spatiotemporal Corruptions
comments: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology (TCSVT). Code and benchmark resources are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhonghuaYi/optical_flow_robustness_benchmark
summary: Optical flow estimation is a fundamental task in dynamic scene understanding and computer vision. While recent deep models achieve impressive accuracy on clean benchmarks, their robustness to common visual and temporal degradations remains insufficiently explored. To address this gap, we establish a real-video-based spatiotemporal corruption benchmark suite that complements rendered and mixed-source robustness benchmarks, systematically evaluating two complementary aspects of visual perception: domain robustness and motion-distribution robustness. We construct two targeted benchmarks: KITTI Flow Corruptions (KITTI-FC) for dynamic outdoor scenes and GoPro Flow Corruptions (GoPro-FC) for diverse first-person-view complex motions. Both benchmarks use captured source data and apply 24 controlled, predominantly algorithmic corruptions encompassing digital, illumination, weather, noise, blur, and video artifacts. To quantify robustness, we use two complementary axes: the GT-free output-stability error Rs and the GT-based accuracy degradation Rd, together with their clean-error-normalized variants. We systematically evaluate 33 model variants from 17 representative optical flow methods. Our results show that, under the evaluated corruption schedules, models exhibit greater vulnerability to local structural information loss (e.g., JPEG compression and spatter) than to global perceptual distortions (e.g., fog and saturation). We further find that in-domain fine-tuning does not guarantee relative robustness and that no single current method dominates across all tested source and motion settings. Our work provides a controlled diagnostic framework for assessing optical flow robustness and developing reliable perception systems in complex environments. Code and benchmark resources are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhonghuaYi/optical_flow_robustness_benchmark.
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology (TCSVT). Code and benchmark resources are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhonghuaYi/optical_flow_robustness_benchmark

title: A General-Purpose Neuromorphic Sensor based on Spiketrum Algorithm: Hardware Details and Real-life Applications
comments: Currently under review in "IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Regular Papers"
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a biologically inspired computational paradigm, enabling energy-efficient data processing through spike-based information transmission. Despite notable advancements in hardware for SNNs, spike encoding has largely remained software-dependent, limiting efficiency. This paper addresses the need for adaptable and resource-efficient spike encoding hardware by presenting an area-optimized hardware implementation of the Spiketrum algorithm, which encodes time-varying analogue signals into spatiotemporal spike patterns. Unlike earlier performance-optimized designs, which prioritize speed, our approach focuses on reducing hardware footprint, achieving a 52% reduction in Block RAMs (BRAMs), 31% fewer Digital Signal Processing (DSP) slices, and a 6% decrease in Look-Up Tables (LUTs). The proposed implementation has been verified on an FPGA and successfully integrated into an IC using TSMC180 technology. Experimental results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in real-world applications, including sound and ECG classification. This work highlights the trade-offs between performance and resource efficiency, offering a flexible, scalable solution for neuromorphic systems in power-sensitive applications like cochlear implants and neural devices.
comment: Currently under review in "IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Regular Papers"

title: Tube-Based Robust Control Strategy for Vision-Guided Autonomous Vehicles
summary: A robust control strategy for autonomous vehicles can improve system stability, enhance riding comfort, and prevent driving accidents. This paper presents a novel interpolation-tubebased constrained iterative linear quadratic regulator (itubeCILQR) algorithm for autonomous computer-vision-based vehicle lane-keeping. The goal of the algorithm is to enhance robustness during high-speed cornering on tight turns. Compared with standard tube-based approaches, the proposed itube-CILQR algorithm reduces system conservatism and exhibits higher computational speed. Numerical simulations and vision-based experiments were conducted to examine the feasibility of using the proposed algorithm for controlling autonomous vehicles. The results indicated that the proposed algorithm achieved superior vehicle lane-keeping performance to variational CILQRbased methods and model predictive control (MPC) approaches involving the use of a classical interior-point optimizer. Specifically, itube-CILQR required an average runtime of 3.45 ms to generate a control signal for guiding a self-driving vehicle. By comparison, itube-MPC typically required a 4.32 times longer computation time to complete the same task. Moreover, the influence of conservatism on system behavior was investigated by exploring the variations in the interpolation variables derived using the proposed itube-CILQR algorithm during lane-keeping maneuvers.

title: Markovian Continuity of the MMSE
comments: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. This version incorporates the revisions made during peer review
summary: Minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation is widely used in signal processing, information theory, and related fields. Despite its practical robustness, the MMSE can be discontinuous under standard notions of stochastic convergence. To bridge this gap, we review classical counterexamples to the continuity of the MMSE and identify two obstructions: failure of second-moment convergence and approximating observations carrying more information about the limit estimand than the limit observation does. Motivated by practical acquisition mechanisms, we study MMSE continuity under two natural constraints: (1) continuity of the second moment, and (2) a degradedness (Markov) restriction ensuring that each approximating observation is no more informative than the limit observation is about the limit estimand. Under these conditions, we establish continuity of the MMSE and of the MMSE estimator. We provide complementary semicontinuity results and continuity guarantees in related settings and establish continuity under linear estimation. We further extend the analysis to the families of Bregman divergences and continuous metric and generalized metric cost functions, including the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences as special cases.
comment: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. This version incorporates the revisions made during peer review

title: A cell problem for the boundary density and approximation of boundary correctors in homogenization theory
summary: We study the boundary corrector $θ_ε$ in the two-scale expansion for periodic elliptic problems with Dirichlet conditions. By results of Gérard-Varet--Masmoudi and Prange, on smooth uniformly convex domains $θ_ε$ converges to the solution $θ^*$ of a homogenized problem with boundary data given by the boundary layer tail $d(n)$, which is determined by a half-space problem for each normal $n$. In the lifted form of Gérard-Varet and Masmoudi, $d(n)$ is given explicitly by the cell correctors and the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator $N_n$ of this half-space problem. Our main result is that $N_n$ satisfies a nonlinear equation on the period cell alone, so that $d(n)$ and the boundary density that represents it can be computed on the cell. This equation is a Riccati equation in which the derivative in depth is replaced by a commutator with the derivative along $n$. This cell problem can therefore be solved by a Riccati doubling algorithm, and we can compute $d(n)$ at irrational normals without rational approximation. Dropping the commutator term in the cell equation gives an operator square root approximation for $N_n$ that captures the leading term of $d(n)$ for small contrast, for the truncated problem. Finally, we approximate $θ_ε$ at finite $ε$ by the sum of two solutions of constant coefficient problems, one with oscillatory boundary data and the other $θ^*$, and test it on the disk.

title: Failure Modes of Interior-Point SDP Solvers on Moment--SOS Hierarchies
summary: Standard semidefinite programming (SDP) solvers working in double precision can become unreliable on difficult problems, even when their output appears plausible. We study this issue for SDP problems arising from high-order moment-SOS hierarchies. Three polynomial optimization problems are analysed by comparing standard double-precision computations with reference solutions obtained using the extended-precision solver \mbox{Loraine\,64x4}. We observe two distinct patterns of numerical failure. In \emph{false convergence}, the computed bounds form a smooth sequence but approach the limit at the wrong rate. In \emph{stagnation}, the sequence develops a plateau or oscillations and no longer reflects the convergence of the underlying hierarchy. We introduce an empirical effective condition number based on the positive spectral components of the primal and dual solution matrices. It serves as a warning indicator rather than an error bound, and its growth accompanies numerical deterioration in our examples. We also examine the imbalance between primal and dual spectral conditioning and a Cholesky inverse residuum as potential diagnostic indicators. The results show that solver termination messages and apparently regular convergence curves may be insufficient to establish the reliability of high-order moment-SOS bounds.

title: Beyond periodicity: Fourier methods for optimal control
summary: Fourier-based spectral methods provide compact global approximations, permit simple differentiation and integration, and achieve spectral convergence for smooth periodic functions. Their use in finite-horizon optimal control problems (OCPs) is nevertheless challenged by the generally nonperiodic state and control trajectories: endpoint mismatch induces artificial discontinuities and can destroy spectral convergence. Leveraging Eckhoff-type endpoint-correction techniques, we develop a Fourier-based spectral framework for OCPs with possibly nonlinear dynamics and constraints. The correction improves convergence without enlarging the set of decision variables, yielding an efficient finite-dimensional numerical method. Furthermore, we formulate selected dynamics and obstacle-avoidance constraints through Sobolev residual bounds, which incorporate information about the residuals over the entire time horizon and improve constraint satisfaction. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate competitive computational performance, lower residual errors, and improved solution accuracy.

title: Fresnel scattering for open waveguide networks
summary: This paper concerns the Helmholtz scattering problem for open waveguide networks, extending the analysis from [arXiv:2302.04353, arXiv:2310.05816, arXiv:2401.04674] to plane-wave incident data. We first reduce the problem to a Fredholm second-kind integral equation on an infinite interface. This produces an integral representation of the solution to the original scattering problem, which is then used to obtain detailed asymptotic estimates of the solution at infinity. To leading order and away from the waveguides, the scattered field is itself a plane wave. Its amplitude and phase shift exhibit a jump across a critical polar angle depending on the direction of the incident plane-wave. Our estimates also imply that the scattered field is outgoing in a weak sense, allowing us to establish a uniqueness result. We conclude by calculating the waveguide-mode contributions to the scattered field in a perturbative regime.

title: One-way pressure-independent valves with hysteresis and chattering
summary: We propose a model for the one-dimensional isothermal gas flow through a valve in a pipe. The valve aims at keeping the outgoing flow in an assigned interval; moreover, its opening and closing depend on a further parameter. The model is realized by a system of two conservation laws with suitable conditions coupling the ingoing and the outgoing flow. We study the corresponding Riemann problem, where non-classical shocks show up. Although simple, the model allows to study two key oscillatory behaviors of the flow, which are due, respectively, to the chattering of the valve, especially seen in the numerical simulations, and to the stabilizing hysteresis induced by the valve operation. We characterize the states leading to chattering and show how they depend on the parameters of the model. Through several numerical simulations, we study the interplay between the two above phenomena.

title: A Projection Anderson Acceleration Algorithm for Non-quasi-monotone Variational Inequalities with Hölder Continuous Terms
summary: This paper proposes a Projection Anderson Acceleration (PAA) algorithm for variational inequality (VI) problems, where the underlying function is expressed as a finite sum of Hölder continuous functions and satisfies the $σ$-star strongly monotone condition that includes the star strong monotonicity with $σ= 1$ as a special case. In the absence of quasi-monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, we establish the evaluation complexity of the PAA algorithm for finding an approximate solution. Specifically, for the star strongly monotone VI problems, the PAA algorithm needs at most $O (\log (ε^{-1}) ε^{2 (\underlineα - 1)})$ evaluations of the function and projection for finding an $ε$-approximate solution, where $\underlineα \in (0, 1]$ is the smallest exponent of H{ö}lder continuity of the component functions. We illustrate our theoretical results by numerical examples of non-quasi-monotone complementarity problems and non-monotone semilinear elliptic equations with non-Lipschitz terms.

title: Orientation Estimation of Cryo-EM Images for Molecules with Arbitrary Symmetry by Semidefinite Programming
summary:
This paper extends the non-unique games framework introduced in Bandeira et al. (2020) to address symmetric structures. Precisely, we consider the problem \[ \begin{aligned}
  \underset{g_1,\ldots,g_n\in \mathcal{G}}{\operatorname{min}}\,\, \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i,j=1}^n \sum_{s\in S} f_{ij}(g_i s g_j^{-1}), \end{aligned} \] where $\mathcal{G}$ is a compact group, $S\subset \mathcal{G}$ is a finite subgroup of symmetry elements, and $f_{ij}:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a loss function. A notable example is common lines based orientation estimation of cryo-EM images for molecules with point group symmetry $S$, where $\mathcal{G}$ is the rotation group $\operatorname{SO}(3)$. With a semidefinite programming relaxation, we turn the problem into a convex program that is solved with the alternating direction method of multipliers. Unlike existing approaches which are tailored to specific symmetry groups, ours provides a unified computational framework for addressing all point group symmetries. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed algorithm on the cryo-EM orientation estimation problem on both simulated and experimental datasets. In particular, our algorithm is effective in generating high-quality ab initio models from only a few class averages computed from experimental images.

title: Sampling with collective variables: Relative error analysis for umbrella sampling under general conditions
summary: We consider the problem of estimating the expectation of a function (observable) with respect to a high-dimensional probability distribution, under the assumption that a low-dimensional collective variable map captures all the directions of slow mixing for the distribution. More precisely, under the assumption that the fibers of the collective variable map satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality, we establish non-asymptotic relative-error guarantees for this problem using the eigenvector method for umbrella sampling (EMUS). Our analysis applies to both log-Lipschitz observables and indicator of convex sets, and gives complexity bounds that are polynomial in regularity parameters and inverse relative accuracy, and exponential in the dimension of the collective variable space. As a relative error guarantee, our bounds apply to rare event estimation. We consider Gaussian biasing windows defined on a low-dimensional collective variable space and analyze a modified sparse matrix version of EMUS. The bounds quantify the effect of the map through mixing of the conditional distribution and fluctuation of the observable along the fibers.

title: Viscosity-uniform error estimates for a semi-implicit Fourier method in Besov spaces
comments: 44 pages, 6 figures. Combined and substantially revised version of arXiv:2406.12320v1 and arXiv:2509.23192v1; title changed; expanded analysis and numerical experiments
summary: We prove error estimates for a semi-implicit Fourier--Galerkin method for two-dimensional incompressible flow on the torus, with viscosity $0\leν\le1$. The temporal error is first order in $H^s$ for $H^{s+2}$ initial data and integer $s\ge1$. For data in $B^m_{2,1}$, with integer $m\ge3$, the fully discrete error is of order $τ+N^{-(m-2)}$ in $B^1_{2,1}$ and $B^0_{\infty,1}$. These estimates hold on a common local interval, with constants and time-step thresholds independent of viscosity and Fourier resolution. For data in $B^{2+\varepsilon}_{2,1}$, $0<\varepsilon<1$, the error relative to Euler flow is bounded by $C(τ^{(1+\varepsilon)/2}+N^{-\varepsilon} +ν^{(1+\varepsilon)/2})$. The consistency bounds use viscosity-weighted regularity. Orthogonality of the Leray and Fourier projectors in the block energies gives the endpoint estimates, and stability with respect to the initial data yields the fractional rate. An $L^2$ residual tolerance $δ$ contributes $CNδ$ to the endpoint error of computed iterates. We report refinement studies for smooth and fixed multiscale data, together with qualitative flow comparisons. An exactly solvable rough shear has fractional errors, up to logarithms, in $B^1_{2,1}$ and first-order errors in $B^0_{\infty,1}$.
comment: 44 pages, 6 figures. Combined and substantially revised version of arXiv:2406.12320v1 and arXiv:2509.23192v1; title changed; expanded analysis and numerical experiments

title: Computational Math with Neural Networks is Hard
summary: We establish asymptotic complexity barriers for three basic numerical tasks with neural-network data: integration of a network realization, solution of a Poisson problem with a neural-network right-hand side, and multiplication by a neural-network encoded matrix. A common reduction encodes Boolean formulas as ReLU networks and reduces Boolean satisfiability to each task. Any algorithm improving on the resulting convergence-rate bounds would contradict the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH). These bounds hold even with full access to the network representation, including all weights. The core reductions use networks with three hidden layers, width linear in the number of Boolean variables, bounded realizations, and sparse connectivity. A finite-precision Monte Carlo quadrature attains the optimal rate for integration up to logarithmic factors, so the lower bound for integration is sharp. We show slightly weaker lower bounds for networks with two hidden layers and provide fast quadrature algorithms for one-hidden-layer networks.

title: On efficient multigrid solvers for mixed-degree local discontinuous Galerkin multiphase Stokes problems
summary: We design and investigate efficient multigrid solvers for multiphase Stokes problems discretised via mixed-degree local discontinuous Galerkin methods. Using the template of a standard multigrid V-cycle, we develop a smoother analogous to element-wise block Gauss-Seidel, except the diagonal block inverses are replaced with an approximation that balances the smoothing of the velocity and pressure variables, factoring in the unequal scaling of the various Stokes system operators, and optimised via two-grid local Fourier analysis. We evaluate the performance of the multigrid solver across an extensive range of two- and three-dimensional test problems, including steady-state and unsteady, standard-form and stress-form, single-phase and high-contrast multiphase Stokes problems, with multiple kinds of boundary conditions and various choices of polynomial degree. In the lowest-degree case, i.e., that of piecewise constant pressure fields, we observe reliable multigrid convergence rates, though not especially fast. However, in every other case, we see rapid convergence rates matching those of classical Poisson-style geometric multigrid methods; e.g., 5 iterations reduce the Stokes system residual by 5 to 10 orders of magnitude.

title: On the Upper Bounds for the Matrix Spectral Norm
summary: We consider the problem of estimating the spectral norm of a matrix using only matrix-vector products. We propose a new Counterbalance estimator that provides upper bounds on the norm and derive probabilistic guarantees on its underestimation. Compared to standard approaches such as the power method, the proposed estimator produces significantly tighter upper bounds in both synthetic and real-world settings. Our method is especially effective for matrices with fast-decaying spectra, such as those arising in deep learning and inverse problems.

title: Dimension of Bi-degree $(d,d)$ Spline Spaces with the Highest Order of Smoothness over Hierarchical T-Meshes
comments: Accepted for publication in SCIENCE CHINA Mathematics, DOI: 10.1007/s11425-023-2499-9
summary: In this article, we study the dimension of the spline space of di-degree $(d,d)$ with the highest order of smoothness over a hierarchical T-mesh $\mathscr T$ using the smoothing cofactor-conformality method. Firstly, we obtain a dimensional formula for the conformality vector space over a tensor product T-connected component. Then, we prove that the dimension of the conformality vector space over a T-connected component of a hierarchical T-mesh under the tensor product subdivision can be calculated in a recursive manner. Combining these two aspects, we obtain a dimensional formula for the bi-degree $(d,d)$ spline space with the highest order of smoothness over a hierarchical T-mesh $\mathscr T$ with mild assumption. Additionally, we provide a strategy to modify an arbitrary hierarchical T-mesh such that the dimension of the bi-degree $(d,d)$ spline space is stable over the modified hierarchical T-mesh. Finally, we prove that the dimension of the spline space over such a hierarchical T-mesh is the same as that of a lower-degree spline space over its CVR graph. Thus, the proposed solution can pave the way for the subsequent construction of basis functions for spline space over such a hierarchical T-mesh.

title: Artifacts of Numerical Integration in Learning Dynamical Systems
summary: In many applications, one needs to learn a dynamical system from its solutions sampled at a finite number of time points. The learning problem is often formulated as an optimization problem over a chosen function class. However, in the optimization procedure, prediction data from generic dynamics requires a numerical integrator to assess the mismatch with the observed data. This paper reveals potentially serious effects of a chosen numerical scheme on the learning outcome. Specifically, the analysis demonstrates that a damped oscillatory system may be incorrectly identified as having "anti-damping" and exhibiting a reversed oscillation direction, even though it adequately fits the given data points. This paper shows that the stability region of the selected integrator will distort the nature of the learned dynamics. Crucially, reducing the step size or raising the order of an explicit integrator does not, in general, remedy this artifact, because higher-order explicit methods have stability regions that extend further into the right half complex plane. Furthermore, it is shown that the implicit midpoint method can preserve either conservative or dissipative properties from discrete data, offering a principled integrator choice even when the only prior knowledge is that the system is autonomous.

title: On the optimization of discrepancy measures
summary:
Points in the unit cube with low discrepancy can be constructed using algebra or, more recently, by direct computational optimization of a criterion. The usual $L_\infty$ star discrepancy is a poor criterion for this because it is computationally expensive and lacks differentiability. Its usual replacement, the $L_2$ star discrepancy, is smooth but exhibits other pathologies shown by J. Matoušek. In an attempt to address these problems, we introduce the \textit{average squared discrepancy} which averages over $2^d$ versions of the $L_2$ star discrepancy anchored in the different vertices of $[0,1]^d$. Not only can this criterion be computed in $O(dn^2)$ time, like the $L_2$ star discrepancy, but also we show that it is equivalent to a weighted symmetric $L_2$ criterion of Hickernell's by a constant factor. We compare this criterion with a wide range of traditional discrepancy measures, and show that only the average squared discrepancy avoids the problems raised by Matoušek. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive numerical study showing in particular that optimizing for the average squared discrepancy leads to strong performance for the $L_2$ star discrepancy, whereas the converse does not hold.
  This version corrects some of the threshold sample sizes n at which random points become better than n repeated points for some discrepancy measures. In particular, the periodic L_2 discrepancy has no repeated point pathology.

title: Higher Order Unfitted Space-Time Methods for Transport Problems
summary: In this article, we present an Unfitted Space-Time Finite Element method for the scalar transport equation posed on moving domains. We consider the case of the domain boundary being transported by the same velocity field as the scalar concentration inside the physical domain. A standard continuous Galerkin Finite element space is considered on a fixed background mesh, as well as tensor product Space-Time elements, which can be discontinuous along time slice boundaries. For the computational geometry, we opt for a spatially second-order accurate approximation variant in the mathematical analysis. In particular, we establish stability in a problem-specific norm and prove a priori error bounds of high order. Numerical examples illustrate these theoretical findings.

title: IGA-LBM: Isogeometric lattice Boltzmann method
comments: Sections 4.2 and 1 describe the distribution functions as expanded in the NURBS basis with derivatives taken by differentiating that basis; the implementation is a little different. A corrected version will follow
summary: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) offers intrinsic parallelism and simple boundary treatment, but Cartesian lattices approximate curved boundaries by stair steps, causing spurious forces and boundary-layer errors. We present an isogeometric collocation lattice Boltzmann method (IGA-LBM) that solves the discrete-velocity BGK system in strong form on body-fitted B-spline and NURBS geometries. Distribution functions are collocated at Greville points, advection is evaluated with high-order operators on the exact spline mapping, and time integration uses a four-stage Runge-Kutta scheme. Exact geometric metrics preserve a uniform free stream to machine precision on curved grids while retaining formal accuracy. The analysis recovers the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with viscosity nu = cs^2 tau and shows that the main isogeometric advantage is exact geometry rather than a new interior stencil. Centered collocation is stabilized by a high-order filter, a physical-node closure restores fourth-order accuracy near clustered walls, and stiff collision limits the explicit step to dt <= 2.785 tau, scaling as O(Re^-1). Tests confirm the predicted accuracy and the O(Ma^2) compressibility floor. Validation covers the Ghia lid-driven cavity, steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder, and a body-fitted NACA0012 airfoil. For the cylinder, recirculation length is within about 9 percent and the Strouhal number within about 2.5 percent of reference values; drag is 6-12 percent above consensus and decreases with refinement, with stable wakes up to Re = 1000. For NACA0012 at Re = 500 and 10 degrees incidence, surface pressure and skin friction agree with reference data within a few percent. The method provides a high-order, free-stream-preserving LBM for curved-boundary flows based on exact B-spline and NURBS geometry, with demonstrated accuracy, stability, and geometric fidelity.
